\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
Our hierarchical estimator adds partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2018heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured endogenous treatment via IV, deriving nonparametric bounds.
\citet{knox2022testing} formalize how ML-learned proxy variables introduce bias in causal estimation; \citet{knox2020administrative} demonstrate how racial misclassification in administrative records biases causal estimates via selection on the mediator.
\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our setting differs because $\hat{Z}$ is a moderator proxy rather than a confounder proxy, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
Blette et al.~\citep{blette2024assessing} handle missing (not misclassified) effect modifier data in cluster-RCTs via multiple imputation rather than confusion-matrix inversion.
Their simulation-driven assessment targets design-based inference for cluster randomization; we target LLM-annotated observational and experimental data and provide a closed-form bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) with an exact $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure.
Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}); our hierarchical estimator adds partial pooling outside the DSL framework.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via IV; \citet{ura2018heterogeneous} extends this to HTE; \citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for confounder proxies.
These address structurally distinct problems---treatment or confounder mismeasurement rather than effect-modifier misclassification (Appendix~\ref{app:related}).

\paragraph{Noisy label learning.}
The $M^{-1}$ correction structure we apply to causal estimands originates in the label noise literature: \citet{natarajan2013learning} derive unbiased loss corrections via the noise transition matrix; \citet{patrini2017making} scale this to deep networks; \citet{cheng2020learning} extend to instance-dependent noise.
These methods correct \emph{training losses} to learn robust classifiers, while we correct \emph{causal estimands}---the confusion matrix serves as a debiasing tool for treatment effect estimation, and the heterogeneity-driven bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) has no analogue in that literature.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Standard confusion-matrix correction for noisy annotations assumes uniform error rates.
3	When this assumption fails---as it routinely does with LLM classifiers, whose error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across subgroups---correction can reverse estimated effect signs.
4	We derive an exact bias identity: global correction introduces subgroup-level bias $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ under symmetric errors (generalizing to a full-matrix form for arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices; Remark~\ref{rem:asymmetric}), verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids ($R^2 = 0.975$ in aggregate across 11 real LLM confusion matrices; per-model range $0.76$--$0.99$).
5	The identity predicts that global correction reverses CATE sign in 14.9\% of configurations where the true effect is small ($\tau(0) = 0.03$) and amplifies bias in all eight real LLMs tested; a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic corollary flags harmful correction from error rates alone, without estimating treatment effects.
6	We characterize when per-subgroup correction is beneficial ($\Delta\pi > 0.15$, $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$, $K \leq 4$) versus when global correction should be retained, and implement one such correction via hierarchical Bayesian estimation, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ by $7.4\times$ under extreme heterogeneity.
7	\end{abstract}
